analysis.one_liner: Replaces drug patents with government prizes so every new medicine can be sold cheaply as a generic.
analysis.headline: Introduced in 2007 by a single senator with no cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Health Committee without a hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended the way new medicines are rewarded in the United States. Instead of giving a drug company a patent — the exclusive right to sell a new medicine at whatever price it chooses — the government would pay companies cash prizes based on how much their innovations actually improve health. In exchange, any company meeting FDA standards could manufacture and sell any approved drug immediately, the way generics do today. The prize fund would be paid for with a permanent appropriation of 0.6 percent of the U.S. economy each year, which the bill's findings claimed would be far outweighed by more than $200 billion a year in savings from lower drug prices. It was referred to the Senate Health Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take prescription drugs, and everyone who helps pay for them — employers who provide insurance, taxpayers who fund Medicare and Medicaid, and the uninsured who pay out of pocket. The bill's findings cite FDA data showing that only about 22 percent of new drug approvals from 1990 to 2004 were for genuinely improved medicines, and it would have redirected innovation rewards toward drugs that help the most patients and address unmet needs, including neglected diseases in poor countries and rare diseases. Generic makers would also have gained immediate access to every approved medicine.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and everyone who pays for medicines

how_it_helps.text: It would have allowed any FDA-compliant manufacturer to produce and sell every approved medicine, ending the exclusive rights that let brand-name companies set high prices [S3].

It would have replaced those exclusive rights with prize payments from a permanent federal fund sized at 0.6 percent of GDP, so companies could still earn money from successful research without the public paying monopoly prices [S3].

It would have required the prize Board to reserve at least 10 percent of the fund for orphan drugs, 4 percent for global neglected diseases, and 4 percent for global infectious diseases — research areas the current patent system serves poorly because patients cannot pay high prices [S3].

It would have paid prizes based on how many patients benefit and how much a drug improves over existing treatments, rather than on sales, redirecting innovation incentives away from me-too marketing toward real therapeutic gains [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the prize fund — a permanent annual appropriation of 0.6 percent of GDP, more than $80 billion in 2007 by the bill's own estimate. Brand-name pharmaceutical companies would lose their exclusive marketing rights and the monopoly prices they support, receiving government prize payments capped at ten years instead. If the savings on drug prices did not materialize as projected, the net cost to taxpayers would be substantial.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug companies and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The prize fund requires a permanent annual appropriation of 0.6 percent of GDP — roughly $80 billion in 2007 — paid from the Treasury whether or not the savings materialize as projected [S3].

Everything depends on a government Board correctly estimating the value of each new medicine; a Board that sets prizes too low could discourage investment in genuinely important new drugs, and one that sets them too high could waste taxpayer money [S3].

The bill eliminates every exclusive marketing right — including orphan drug exclusivity, pediatric extensions, and the 30-month stay that blocks generic challenges — effective October 1, 2007, with no gradual phase-in for existing business models built on patent exclusivity [S3].

Brand-name companies could receive prize payments for at most 10 fiscal years per drug, capped at 5 percent of the annual fund, so a blockbuster with decades of remaining patent life could be compensated far less than its current market value [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential payoff was enormous: Congress's own findings in the bill put current drug spending at over $274 billion in 2006 and claimed the switch could save more than $200 billion a year, far more than the roughly $80 billion a year the prize fund would cost [S3]. The honest drawbacks are serious, though. The prize fund is a permanent new entitlement sized to 0.6 percent of GDP, so its cost is fixed regardless of how well the Board performs [S3]. Everything hinges on a thirteen-member Board accurately judging how valuable each new medicine is; rewarding too little could discourage investment in new drugs, and rewarding too much could waste taxpayer money [S3]. And the transition — ending every existing exclusive marketing right on a single date — would be the most sweeping change to pharmaceutical incentives ever attempted, with real uncertainty about how research investment would respond. Even supporters would concede the design risk was large; opponents never had to engage with it, because the bill never got a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: One senator introduced it, not a single colleague signed on, the Senate Health Committee never took it up, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on October 19, 2007, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1, S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded — and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies are better off, because they kept the patent exclusivity and monopoly pricing the bill would have ended, and no other member of Congress had to take a position on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept exclusive pricing

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 19, 2007 and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 19, 2007 and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry holding patent-based exclusive marketing rights
against.what_they_did: The research-based drug industry has consistently opposed proposals to replace patent exclusivity with prize funds or to shorten the period of exclusive pricing, the core of what this bill would have ended.

against.name: U.S. Senate
against.what_they_did: Not a single senator from either party cosponsored the bill, and the Senate never considered it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator from either party signed on, so there was no visible partisan division — only one independent senator acting alone.

industries.note: The bill eliminated patent rights and exclusive marketing periods for all drugs and biologics, which are the foundation of brand-name companies' pricing power and profit, replacing them with government prize payments capped at 10 years per product [S3]. Under the current system, exclusive rights are what allow these companies to charge prices far above the cost of production.

With exclusive rights eliminated, any compliant manufacturer could immediately produce every approved medicine, dramatically expanding the generic market that already accounts for 63 percent of prescriptions but only 20 percent of drug spending [S3].

Federal spending on medicines through Medicare, Medicaid, the VA, the Defense Department, and other programs was expected to exceed $100 billion in 2007; the bill's findings claimed government savings alone would more than fund the prize fund [S3]. Lower drug prices would relieve federal and state budgets.

industries.industry: Medical research funders and nonprofit R&D
industries.note: The bill required minimum prize funding for neglected diseases, orphan drugs, and global infectious diseases, channels that could direct money toward research the current market ignores. But the nonprofit sector would also have had to compete for a government Board's judgment of their innovations' value rather than selling exclusive rights.
